I do feel like I need to point out that I feel like the wall is a stupid idea, though by the numbers you posted it is quite cheap. It will be much more expensive to build in the real world because much of the border is underlain by bentonite clays, and the Rio Grande needs to meander.

Bentonites swell when water is added to them. They swell a lot, sometimes expanding to 2 - 3 times their original size. This plays hell on the foundations of buildings, as the ground below them expands and contracts by 2 - 3 times it's normal size every time it rains. Building the wall on top of that is going to present some very unique challenges that are going to raise the cost of building the wall considerably.

The Rio Grande meandering is a problem because restricting it will lower the elevation of the areas where it's restricted. Erosion and deposition of soils in rivers is a pretty easy thing to understand. When water moves uphill, it looses energy and deposits any sediment it's carrying. When it moves downhill, it picks up energy and picks up sediment on the floor of the river. The height that dictates what is uphill and downhill is the elevation of the river at it's mouth (most often sea level). When the Mississippi was forced through the dikes in New Orleans the river could no longer meander as it would naturally (eroding and depositing sediment throughout the flood plane). Instead the river is stuck in one narrow part of the Mississippi delta. This is one of the largest rivers in the world, so naturally it carries a lot of sediment in it. The water hits the dikes and speeds up (greater flow through lower area), but once it leaves the dikes it slows down and dumps all the sediment into the delta. Sediment has weight, and tectonic plates actually float on top of rocks in the mantle that have the consistency of really really really dense jello. That means that where there is more weight on a plate, it sinks. The weight pushes the delta down, which pushes New Orleans to a lower sea level. Not only this, but it pushes the Mississippi river down to a lower sea level than at its mouth, which means that it is loosing power, and depositing the sediment which pushes the delta down ever further in a feedback loop.

Assuming that the wall is built on the American side of the Rio Grande, and that the bentonites + occasional flooding don't destroy it, there will definitely be unforeseen consequences of building the wall.
